title: Proline-promoted electrophilic dichloromethylation of α-enaminones via stereochemically gated resolution

paper_content.abstract:
The direct incorporation of polyhalomethyl groups into carbonyl frameworks has traditionally relied on radical or
carbene intermediates. Here, we report a proline-mediated, closed-shell strategy for electrophilic β-
polyhalomethylation of α-enaminones using stable haloforms under mild, metal-free conditions. The reaction
proceeds with high diastereoselectivity, governed by a stereoelectronic gating mechanism that links molecular
topology to productive C-C bond formation. The platform accommodates a broad range of CX₂ donors, including
CHBr₃, CHBr₂Cl, and CBrCl₃, and reveals topology-dependent divergence: six-membered α-enaminones yield
isolable β-functionalized products, while five-membered analogues engage in a spontaneous cascade, triggered
by reaction with proline, culminating in aromatized benzenoid scaffolds. Structural, isotopic, and spectroscopic
studies support a unique reactivity manifold defined by polarity inversion and closed-shell transfer. This work
redefines electrophilic halomethane chemistry, establishes a mechanistic class for β-functionalization, and
positions α-enaminones as versatile, programmable platforms for topology-driven reactivity and downstream
synthetic elaboration.
paper_content.introduction:
Organocatalysis has transformed modern synthetic chemistry by enabling precise carbonyl functionalization under
mild, metal-free conditions, with enamine catalysis occupying a central conceptual role.1 Yet a persistent and
largely unaddressed contradiction underlies this framework: carbonyl compounds bearing α-hydroxy or α-amino
substituents, motifs that appear ideally suited for enamine activation, consistently resist engagement with
secondary amine catalysts. Despite decades of methodological development, these α-substituted ketones remain
effectively inert under canonical organocatalytic conditions, revealing a fundamental limitation in how carbonyl
reactivity is currently conceptualized.2,3

Our previous studies established that this failure is intrinsic rather than circumstantial. Both α-hydroxy and α-
amino ketones reproducibly fail to form productive enamines, independent of catalyst identity or reaction
conditions. This systematic inertness indicates that classical enamine logic is fundamentally incompatible with
these scaffolds and suggests that selective functionalization of these scaffolds cannot be achieved through
incremental modification of existing organocatalytic strategies. Instead, it points to the existence of an alternative,
unrecognized reactivity regime embedded within α-substituted carbonyl architectures.2,3

Guided by this realization, we sought to identify non-canonical activation modes that exploit, rather than
circumvent, the stereoelectronic constraints imposed by α-substitution. This effort revealed a unifying mechanistic
principle across α-oxygenated and α-aminated ketones: reactivity arises from geometrically enforced polarity
inversion rather than from enamine formation. In this framework, closed-shell cascades convert structural
constraints into chemical driving forces. We demonstrated that α-hydroxy ketones undergo metal-free reductive
dehydroxylation via hydroxylamine intermediates (Figure 1A).2 In contrast, α,β-unsaturated α-aminoketones
undergo decarboxylative condensation cascades, yielding previously inaccessible polycyclic ionic liquids (Figure
1B).3 Although distinct in outcome, these transformations share a common logic in which reactivity is dictated by
stereoelectronic gating and intramolecular acid-base choreography rather than by classical nucleophile-
electrophile pairing (Figure 1C). Together, these findings redefine α-substituted carbonyls as programmable
platforms for polarity-driven reactivity.

Within this emerging paradigm, we now report a third and conceptually distinct transformation: the closed-shell,
electrophilic β-dichloromethylation of α-enaminoketones using unmodified halomethanes (Figure 1D). This
reaction enables direct C-C bond formation from simple haloform-type reagents under mild conditions, without
metals, radicals, carbenes, light, or preactivation. Under proline-buffered conditions (L-proline, K₃PO₄, CHBrCl₂),
α-enaminones undergo site- and stereoselective installation of a CHCl₂ unit at the β-position, delivering densely
functionalized scaffolds that combine a ketone, a tertiary amine, and a synthetically versatile dihalomethyl handle
in a single operation. The transformation proceeds with complete anti-stereoselectivity (>99:1) across a broad
substrate range and exhibits a characteristic yield ceiling that reflects intrinsic mechanistic partitioning rather than
incomplete conversion.

Mechanistic analysis reveals that this behavior arises from a diastereomer-resolved bifurcation at the
hydroxylamine stage. Reaction of the α-enaminone with proline generates two transient intermediates, only one
of which adopts a geometry permissive for decarboxylation and electrophilic CHCl₂ incorporation. The
mismatched diastereomer enters a kinetically stable off-cycle state and fragments cleanly upon workup. This
stereochemically gated resolution defines a previously unrecognized mode of reactivity control, in which molecular
topology rather than catalyst chirality governs productive bond formation. Comprehensive isotopic labeling,
fragment reactivity studies, and crystallographic analysis collectively exclude enamine, iminium, radical, or
carbene pathways, establishing a strictly closed-shell mechanism in which polarity inversion and stereoelectronic
gating enable electrophilic halomethyl transfer onto an electronically ambivalent β-carbon center.

The precise incorporation of di- and trihalomethyl groups (CX₂, CX₃) remains a central challenge in synthetic
chemistry, constrained mainly by a fundamental mechanistic dichotomy. Classical approaches rely on highly
reactive dichlorocarbene intermediates, require strong bases, and exhibit poor functional group tolerance.4,5 More
contemporary strategies leverage photoredox catalysis or transition metals to activate halomethanes via radical
pathways, yet these are inherently dependent on single-electron transfer or metal catalysis.6 Critically, both
carbenoid and radical methods predominantly target substrates with rigidly fixed -electron distributions, such as
electron-rich alkenes,7-11 enones,12 or acrylamides,13-15 where conjugation with electron-withdrawing groups
ensures predictable electrophilic capture (Figure 2A).16-20 This bias inherently limits their applicability, leaving a
vast domain of electronically dynamic systems unaddressed.

a-Enaminones represent a prime example of such an unaddressed frontier. Their β-position, governed by
resonance, exhibits a unique electronic ambivalence, capable of inverting between nucleophilic and electrophilic
character depending on the stereoelectronic context.3,21 This inherent dynamism, a source of unique reactivity,
simultaneously renders them recalcitrant to existing halomethylation methods, as their flexible polarization
fundamentally disrupts the fixed -electron demand of established carbene and radical protocols (Figure 2A).

Here, we invert the conventional strategy: rather than forcing α-enaminones into canonical reactivity modes or
circumventing their electronic ambivalence, we harness their electronic ambivalence as a design principle(Figure
2B). Under proline-buffered conditions, α-enaminones undergo closed-shell, β-selective dihalomethylation,
enabling direct C-C bond formation with dihalomethanes in the absence of metals, radicals, light, or carbenes.
This mechanistically distinct transformation allows the selective installation of CHCl₂ units onto electronically
neutral β-carbons. The platform extends to a broader class of polyhalomethyl donors, including CBrCl₃, CHBr₃,
and CHBr₂Cl (Figure 2C), establishing a generalizable framework for CX₂ transfer. Notably, the manifold reveals
latent cascade behavior shaped by subtle stereoelectronic and topological cues.

Together, these results reposition halomethane activation as a polarity-gated, closed-shell process and elevate α-
enaminones as programmable platforms for stereoelectronically choreographed reaction design.
paper_content.results:
Discovery and optimization of α-Enaminone β-Dichloromethylation.
The initial discovery of this transformation emerged during a thermal evaluation of α-enaminone 1 with
stoichiometric L-proline in neat chloroform at 100 °C. This serendipitous finding led to the formation of the β-
dichloromethylated product 2 in a limited yet unambiguous manner (Table 1). Despite the low efficiency of this
initial observation, rigorous characterization by NMR spectroscopy, GC-MS analysis, and single-crystal X-ray
diffraction unequivocally established site-selective -incorporation of the CHCl₂ unit with strict anti-
stereochemistry relative to the pendant amine. This reactivity, the direct installation of a CHCl₂ group onto an α-
enaminone, prompted a comprehensive evaluation of reaction parameters.

Our optimization studies systematically explored the halomethane source, base identity, proline loading, solvent,
temperature, additives, atmosphere, and light exposure. These efforts converged on a narrow, optimal regime
employing CHBrCl₂ (5 equiv.), L-proline (2 equiv.), and K₃PO₄ (1 equiv.) in CHCl₃ at 100 °C for 20 h.

Under these optimized conditions, the transformation proceeded reproducibly, exhibiting clean product profiles
and providing synthetically useful yields. Importantly, no alternative permutation, including the original chloroform-
only conditions, approached this level of performance.

To definitively establish the origin of the dichloromethyl fragment, we conducted targeted isotopic tracing
experiments. Using CHBrCl₂ as the donor in CDCl₃ as solvent, analysis by ¹H/²H NMR spectroscopy and high-
resolution mass spectrometry revealed only minimal incorporation of CDCl₂, despite the large excess of
deuterated solvent. This robustly confirms CHBrCl₂ as the sole operative CHCl₂ source under the optimized
conditions. Further controls demonstrated the reaction's insensitivity to ambient light (excluding UV) and its
efficient operation under open-flask conditions. Additives, including molecular sieves, phase transfer agents, and
acid scavengers (e.g., proton sponges and ion-exchange resins), provided no improvement and, in some cases,
marginally suppressed reactivity, indicating that the system operates effectively under its native, self-buffered
conditions.

A Stereochemically gated resolution pathway to product formation.
Under the optimized conditions, the reaction exhibits high chemo- and site-selectivity; however, product 2 (Table
1) consistently plateaus at approximately 50% yield despite full substrate consumption. This reproducible ceiling
was a critical early mechanistic clue, suggesting an intrinsic constraint rather than incomplete conversion or
product instability.

To investigate these temporal dynamics, we monitored reaction progress and found that, although substrate
consumption proceeded to completion, product formation consistently plateaued at ~50% conversion. This
divergence reflects a non-classical outcome: only a defined subset of reactive intermediates evolves productively.
This observation, coupled with further mechanistic investigations detailed below, led us to propose a resolution-
type pathway as the fundamental determinant of the observed yield ceiling. The full conversion/yield profile, along
with its detailed mechanistic implications, is provided in the Supplementary Section 6.

To account for the divergent reactivity observed, we propose a stereochemically gated mechanism in which the
α-enaminone (3) reacts with L-proline, generating two diastereomeric hydroxylamine intermediates (Figure 3A).
These species, 4a and 4b, differ in their configuration and topology, predisposing them to either productive
transformation or kinetic arrest.

In the productive trajectory, intermediate 4b adopts a conformation in which the α-hydroxyl and proline carboxyl
group are spatially separated, enabling intramolecular proton transfer to the adjacent nitrogen and forming a
transient ammonium intermediate (7). This species undergoes α-decarboxylation, triggering a cascade of electron
flow that restores a nucleophilic enamine system. Substitution with CHBrCl₂ forms a β-dichloromethylated
enolamine (9), with elimination of pyrroline (8) as a byproduct.22

A capture experiment (see Supplementary Section 7) confirmed the formation of pyrroline (8) in situ, which
subsequently oligomerizes to its known trimeric condensate, consistent with literature reports.23 Final
tautomerization yields product (10) with a defined anti-configuration relative to the pendant amine. This outcome
was unambiguously confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction.24

In contrast, intermediate 4a adopts a compact, bridged topology stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonding
between the α-hydroxyl group and proline’s carboxylate. This conformation suppresses both proton transfer and
enamine delocalization, rendering the β-position electronically inert and stalling the cascade.

No reversion to the α-enaminone or formation of a dehydrated intermediate (e.g., 6) was detected throughout the
reaction course by NMR or mass spectrometry. Upon aqueous workup, or, in some cases, during chromatographic
purification, the sequestered species undergoes clean fragmentation into the corresponding 1,2-diketone and
secondary amine. This post-reaction decomposition confirms the off-cycle nature of intermediate 4a and accounts
for the observed recovery, thereby further substantiating the proposed bifurcation model.

This stereochemical divergence, in which only one diastereomeric intermediate proceeds through the cascade
while the other becomes kinetically trapped, establishes the transformation as a resolution-type process.

Part B of Figure 3 addresses and experimentally excludes a mechanistic scenario in which the α-enaminone
undergoes proline-promoted dehydration to form an enamine-iminium intermediate (11), leading to β-substitution
with CHBrCl₂. If operative, this pathway would give rise to a series of electrophilic adducts (12, 13, 14) that
ultimately hydrolyze to a dichloromethylated diketone 15. Although 15 was detectable by NMR in crude mixtures,
it could not be isolated and was not observed by GC or high-resolution mass spectrometry. These findings indicate
that, if formed, the compound exists only in trace amounts and does not accumulate under the reaction conditions.
Taken together, the data strongly disfavor the enamine–iminium route as a productive pathway for this
transformation.

To experimentally substantiate the proposed resolution-type mechanism and account for the post-reaction mass
balance, we examined the crude mixture obtained from the dichloromethylation of α-enaminone 16, derived from
4-chlorophenyl-N-methylmethanamine and 1,2-cyclohexanedione (Figure 3C). 1H NMR analysis revealed
complete consumption of the starting material, yielding a clean 1:1 ratio of the β-dichloromethylated product 17
and the corresponding secondary amine precursor 18.

These findings support a stereochemically gated process in which diastereomeric intermediates are formed in
equal proportion. One is funneled through productive β-functionalization, while the other undergoes post-reaction
fragmentation, releasing the parent amine. This divergence is likely driven by acid- or water-mediated cleavage
during the cascade, consistent with the reaction profile. Although minor resonances of the parent diketone are
observed, its low abundance suggests rapid secondary engagement with excess proline, generating polar adducts
that are removed from the CHCl₃ phase upon workup. Crucially, the absence of detectable competing side
products upon rigorous crude analysis directly underscores the exceptional selectivity of the process. The strict
1:1 product-to-recovered amine ratio constitutes direct evidence for a resolution-type mechanism with
stereochemically defined reactivity.

Experimental investigation of the reaction mechanism.
To probe the structural features essential for reactivity, we subjected the two key fragments of the α-enaminone
scaffold, the parent cyclohexenone and its corresponding enamine, to the optimized dichloromethylation
conditions with CHBrCl₂ (Figure 4A). Neither substrate underwent any detectable transformation, ruling out
classical enamine chemistry or fragment-level nucleophilic or electrophilic engagement. In contrast, the β-
dichloromethylation proceeds cleanly only with the intact enaminone, indicating that its conjugated, ambident
electronic structure is essential for activation under closed-shell conditions. This finding corroborates our prior
observations that α-hydroxy and α-amino ketones resist proline-promoted enamine formation, further highlighting
the mechanistic divergence of α-enaminones from conventional enamine systems.2,3

To probe the mechanism of dichloromethylation, we carried out targeted experiments to assess the proposed
resolution-type divergence pathway (Figure 4) and establish whether CHCl₂ incorporation proceeds via a polar,
closed-shell process. Replacing CHBrCl₂ with CDCl₃ under standard conditions (Figure 4B) led to clean formation
of the β-deuterodichloromethylated product (2a), with full retention of deuterium confirmed by NMR and GC-MS
(see Supplementary Section 9). The incorporation of an intact CDCl₂ unit is consistent with electrophilic
substitution and excludes a carbene-based mechanism, which would be expected to induce isotopic scrambling
or partial deuterium loss.

Furthermore, a control experiment conducted under light-exclusion conditions yielded an identical product
distribution and conversion, indicating that photochemical initiation does not contribute to the transformation.
Collectively, these findings delineate a mechanistic route that departs from established CHCl₂ transfer pathways.
The transformation proceeds without free carbene intermediates (CCl₂) or enamine-type nucleophiles, instead
relying on direct electrophilic activation of CDCl₃ in the presence of the α-enaminone scaffold under proline
catalysis. This closed-shell, conjugation-gated process defines a reactivity mode not captured by existing
dichloromethylation methods.

Further support for the proposed mechanistic bifurcation arises from the stereochemical outcome of the
transformation. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis of the β-dichloromethylated product 2 revealed a defined
anti-configuration between the CHCl₂ group and the pendant amine (Figure 4C).24 This stereospecific termination
is only consistent with the trajectory of the enolamine intermediate 9 proposed in the productive resolution pathway
(Figure 3). No alternative mechanistic scenario, including those involving carbene intermediates or enamine–
iminium equilibration, can rationalize the observed selective anti-selectivity. This crystallographic evidence thus
provides direct structural validation for the sequence of intermediate states inferred from kinetic and resolution-
based studies.

To probe the stereochemical partitioning proposed in Figure 4, we conducted the reaction using an equimolar
mixture of L- and D-proline (1 equiv. each; Figure 4D) under optimized conditions. Complete consumption of the
α-enaminone was observed, yet the reaction plateaued at approximately 50% yield. This result is consistent with
the formation of four diastereomeric hydroxylamine intermediates, two derived from each proline enantiomer,
only half of which undergo productive dichloromethylation. The remaining diastereomers persist as stable, off-cycle
species and are hydrolyzed during workup to regenerate the parent dione and secondary amine.

The observation that complete conversion of the starting material yields only half the product supports a
stoichiometric resolution-type scenario, in which both enantiomers of proline are required to form the full set of
intermediates. While this stereochemical divergence governs reactivity at the hydroxylamine stage, all chiral
information is ultimately lost upon formation of the enolamine intermediate, which precedes product formation. As
such, the process remains racemic, despite proceeding through diastereomerically differentiated intermediates.
Despite the use of enantiopure L-proline, the -dichloromethylation proceeds without asymmetric induction, and
the CHCl₂-bearing stereocenter is formed as a racemate, as confirmed by X-ray crystallography (see
Supplementary Section 10).

The mechanistic indispensability of proline was further clarified through targeted structural modifications.
Replacement of its α-proton with a methyl group (Figure 4E) generated a quaternary center incapable of
decarboxylation,3 resulting in complete loss of reactivity under standard conditions. This outcome directly supports
the requirement for α-decarboxylation and confirms that such elimination is precluded from a fully substituted
center.

Next, to isolate the role of the carboxylic acid, the proline core was substituted with either a methyl ester or a
primary amide (Figure 4G). In both cases, the transformation failed to proceed. These results highlight the second
essential function of the acid: to engage in an intramolecular acid–base interaction with the α-enaminone, forming
an ammonium intermediate that is necessary to drive the cascade. In the absence of either the α-proton or the
free carboxyl group, the system remains inert. Together, these observations establish that decarboxylation and
proton transfer are both mechanistic prerequisites for productive β-dichloromethylation.

The structural demands of the transformation were further dissected by evaluating individual amino acid variants
under the optimized conditions (Figure 4H). The following examples illustrate how deviations from proline’s unique
geometry compromise reactivity. For instance, N-methyl-L-alanine (24), a flexible linear amino acid, yielded only
12% of product formation. Its open-chain geometry lacks the conformational restriction necessary to stabilize the
key hydroxylamine-ammonium intermediate, thereby hindering efficient progression through the reaction
manifold. In contrast, (S)-azetidine-2-carboxylic acid, despite its cyclic constraint, failed to promote reactivity due
to excessive ring strain (23) and unfavorable spatial arrangement between the carboxyl and amino groups,
precluding formation of the internal acid–base stabilized intermediate. Pipecolic acid (25) provided the highest
level of reactivity among all tested variants, affording 15% of the desired product. However, its reduced efficiency
relative to proline likely reflects a limitation at the decarboxylation step: the six-membered ring does not support
the geometric requirements for CO₂ loss under the reaction conditions.3

Collectively, these results underscore that both intramolecular ammonium stabilization and decarboxylation
readiness are essential features governing productive β-dichloromethylation.

The lack of reactivity in α-enaminones bearing aniline derivatives (Figure 4F) further supports the proposed
mechanism. These substrates fail to undergo β-dichloromethylation, likely due to the diminished basicity of the
aniline nitrogen, which prevents formation of the key intramolecular ammonium intermediate 7 (Figure 3A). This
result reinforces the requirement for nitrogen basicity to enable α-decarboxylation and initiate a productive
cascade.

Evaluation of proline analogues 26–29 (Figure 4I) reveals a clear structure-reactivity relationship in the
dichloromethylation cascade. Analogues that preserve the core proline anchor, a five-membered ring bearing a
carboxylic acid and a secondary amine, retain activity, albeit with varying efficiency. The bicyclic derivative (26,
8%), the fused aryl analogue (27, 28%), and the cyclohexane-substituted scaffold (28, 32%) all afford product
formation under standard conditions, indicating tolerance to steric bulk and topological modification.

In contrast, the OH- or OTBS-substituted prolines 29a and 29b, bearing syn and anti γ-positions, respectively,
were completely inactive. We attribute this loss of reactivity to inhibition of the decarboxylation step, likely arising
from a combination of electron-donating effects and intramolecular hydrogen bonding. These features may
stabilize the carboxylate form and prevent access to the required geometry for CO₂ extrusion. Taken together,
these results highlight that while the proline anchor accommodates significant structural variation, substituents
that perturb electronic distribution or conformational flexibility at the γ-position can disrupt key activation steps
and render the system unreactive.

The unique reactivity observed in the discovered transformation was strictly dependent on the presence of K₃PO₄
as the base. Other inorganic and organic bases, including carbonates, acetates, amines, and stronger alkoxides,
uniformly failed to support the formation of the product. The critical role of K₃PO₄ likely stems from its dual function
as a moderately basic, non-nucleophilic inorganic salt and a buffering agent capable of sustaining the narrow
acid–base equilibrium necessary for cascade initiation. Specifically, its basicity appears to promote the formation
of the key proline-derived ammonium intermediate 7 (Figure 3A) through controlled proton transfer to the α-
enaminone, without over-deprotonating the substrate or destabilizing sensitive intermediates. In contrast, weaker
bases are insufficient to initiate this process, while stronger or less selective bases may disrupt the delicate
balance required for α-decarboxylation or induce degradation of CHBrCl₂. The inability of other bases to replicate
the reaction outcome underscores the crucial role of K₃PO₄ in maintaining the precise reactivity window necessary
for -dichloromethylation.

Scope.
The scope of this electrophilic -dichloromethylation manifold was evaluated across a structurally diverse panel
of -enaminones (Figure 5). Under optimized conditions, substrates bearing benzylic, aliphatic, and heterocyclic
N-substituents underwent clean and selective transformation. Products were consistently obtained as single
diastereomers with exclusive anti-configuration between the -CHCl₂ group and the pendant amine, as confirmed
by ¹H NMR spectroscopy and unambiguously validated by single-crystal X-ray diffraction of representative
compound 2. No syn-diastereomers were detected (>99:1 dr), underscoring the high fidelity of the proline-
mediated stereochemical gating. The isolated yields for these adducts (up to 42%) are consistent with the intrinsic
resolution mechanism governing the reaction. As detailed above, the reaction path bifurcates: ~50% of the
racemic substrate enters the productive cascade. At the same time, the remainder is channeled into a non-
productive, off-cycle state that fragments cleanly upon workup. This trade-off ensures high diastereoselectivity
and operational simplicity without the need for complex chiral auxiliaries or transition metals.

We further probed the electronic and steric limits of the nitrogen substituent. Substrates bearing functionalized or
heteroatom-containing N-residues (e.g., compounds 42, 45, 46) were well-tolerated, demonstrating compatibility
with polar functionality. Conversely, sterically bulky N-tert-butyl analogs proved synthetically inaccessible due to
intrinsic substrate instability. These results define a predictable scope for the -dichloromethylation manifold
centered on secondary amine-derived enaminones.

Electrophilic generality: beyond dichloromethylation.
To challenge the broader applicability of this "electrophilic haloform" activation mode, we examined whether the
proline-buffered conditions could mediate the transfer of alternative polyhalomethyl units. Selected -enaminones
were exposed to a panel of haloform-type donors, including CHBr₃, CHClBr₂, and CBrCl₃. Remarkably, under
unmodified conditions, each reagent cleanly furnished the corresponding gem-dibromo, mixed gem-halide, or
polyhalogenated adduct (Figure 6A). To the best of our knowledge, the direct, closed-shell transfer of di- or
trihalomethyl units from these stable reagents to conjugated carbonyl systems is without precedent, establishing
this protocol as a generalizable platform for electrophilic gem-dihalomethylation.

Ring size divergence and aromatization cascade.
Expanding beyond six-membered rings, our investigation into ring-size effects revealed a profoundly divergent
transformation for five-membered -enaminones, contrasting sharply with the inherent instability observed in
seven-membered analogs under the reaction conditions. Upon initial dichloromethylation, these five-membered
substrates rapidly trigger a complex, proline-orchestrated cascade dictated by their unique constrained topology
(Figure 6B). The resulting dichloromethylated intermediate (64) first undergoes rapid condensation with proline to
form a transient enamine (65), which subsequently tautomerizes to a highly reactive iminium species. Crucially,
subsequent deprotonation generates a stabilized azomethine ylide (68),25 characterized by a potent carbanionic
center adjacent to the iminium nitrogen. This strategically positioned ylide then initiates a sequence of skeletal
rearrangements, involving the formation of a pyrrolidine-fused intermediate (70), culminating in spontaneous ring
expansion (71), elimination (72), and aromatization. The net outcome is the formation of densely substituted
aromatic products that bear both pyrrolidine and benzylamine motifs (73). This intricate, topology-dependent
pathway, conspicuously absent in larger ring systems, highlights a fundamental bifurcation in reactivity within the
enaminone manifold and offers a concise, metal-free route to complex aromatic architectures from structurally
simple cyclic precursors.

Synthetic utility and derivatization. To underscore the synthetic potential of these adducts, we demonstrated
the versatility of the -dichloromethylated synthon as a functional linchpin. Downstream transformations afforded
diverse functionalities, including an (E)-configured vinyl chloride, a ketal, an acetal, and an enol ether (Figure 6C).
These examples demonstrate the utility of the installed gem-dihalomethyl motif as a gateway to structural
complexity.12,26

The conversion of the CHCl₂ group to the corresponding aldehyde,27 further extends this reactivity space: the
resulting carbonyl condenses efficiently with primary amines derived from Amphenicol (79) and Tryptamine
(80),28,29 enabling rapid assembly of hybrid structures that integrate β-dichloromethyl enaminone cores with
bioactive motifs (Figure 6D). Collectively, these results establish the CHCl₂ unit as a strategically reconfigurable
handle for skeletal editing and late-stage conjugation to complex small-molecule architectures.
paper_content.methods:
General procedure for dichloromethylation of α-enaminones.
To a reaction tube equipped with a magnetic stir bar were added proline (2.0 equiv., 0.6 mmol, 69.2 mg), K₃PO₄
(1.0 equiv., 0.3 mmol, 63.7 mg), the corresponding α-enaminone (1.0 equiv., 0.3 mmol), and chloroform (0.075 M,
4 mL), followed by bromodichloromethane (5.0 equiv., 1.5 mmol). The tube was then tightly sealed, and the
mixture was stirred at 100 °C for 10-72 h. After cooling to room temperature, the reaction mixture was concentrated
under reduced pressure, and the crude was purified by chromatography to afford the corresponding
dichloromethylated product.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Tsvelikhovsky et al report the β-dichloromethylation of α-enaminones mediated by proline to obtain the trans- addition product via a novel, closed-shell mechanism. This transformation is very elegant and represents the first dichloromethylation of a typically underexplored class of substrates. I believe this work is suitable for publication in Nature Communications once the following points have been addressed.
1) The authors stipulate that the reaction was conducted in the absence of light, however in the supporting information there is no indication that the reaction was conducted under ‘dark’ conditions i.e. wrapped in foil and whether this affects the yield of the reaction.
2) ‘kinetic profiling’ was conducted however, no orders in reagents etc have been reported and from what I gather from Figure 3 is that the conversion of the reaction was monitored rather than rate.
3) I personally found figure 3 in its current form confusing, I like the idea of summarizing the results but surely an optimization table (like the one in the supporting information) gives the same information.
4) Could the authors comment if they observed the proposed pyrroline decomposition product from the proline rather than just citing the literature. This should be identifiable via GCMS and 1H NMR spectroscopy.
5) There is some colloquial language being used throughout (e.g. NMR which should be NMR spectroscopy etc).
6) The authors mention that initial findings were carried out using CHCl3 as solvent but a higher yield was observed using HCCl2Br. Can the CHCl3 be ruled out as the source of ‘HCCl2’ given the high concentration of CHCl3 in comparison to HCCl2Br? Also, the isotope labelling was conducted using CDCl3 without the use of HCCl2Br – would looking at the Singleton type KIE measurements be more useful in the mechanistic determination rather than the 1H/2H isotope labelling study.
7) On page 6 of the manuscript, it is stated that complete conversion of starting material is observed, yielding a clean 1:1 ratio of the desired product 17 and the corresponding secondary amine. I was wondering if you observe the other fragment from the unproductive pathway?
8) On page 8, when other bases were screened, was any dichlorocarbene addition products (gem-dichlorocyclopropanation) or carbene dimerization products (C2Cl4) observed.
9) The substrate scope demonstrates the ability to change the amine/enamine fragment but the enone fragment remains as a 6-memebered ring, could the authors comment on if smaller/larger ring systems would also work. Also could the authors comment on why only a single addition to the α-enaminones (product 45) when there are two initially identical sites for reactivity and does this have something to do with the low isolated yield for this compound?
10) In the supplementary information, some of the compound characterization needs addressing, especially the 1H NMR spectroscopic data. If a signal has a defined multiplicity, then it needs to have a coupling constant. If it is a multiplet, then a range with no coupling constant should be reported.
11) Starting material 2-((4-methoxybenzyl)(methyl)amino)cyclohex-2-en-1-one is missing a proton in the characterization. This compound should have 19 protons but only 18 are reported.
12) It would be nice for compound 2a to if a 2H NMR spectrum was obtained to make sure there is deuterium incorporated in the compound.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Tsvelikhovsky and co-workers reported the proline-promoted dichloromethylation of α-enaminones via stereochemically gated resolution. The selective β-dichloromethylation of α-enaminones was achieved with anti-stereochemistry. However, the yield of target product is two low (from 42%-6%) along with the decomposition of the enaminones. The low yield of this conversation largely decreased the practicality of this reaction. The current required further optimizations.
Other comments 1. Why the reaction plateaued at 50% yield when using an equimolar mixture of L- and D-proline? While product 2 was obtained in 30% yield in the presence of only L-prolin?
2. CHCl3 can also be used as the CHCl2 source as listed in Figure 3. So, how can the authors deem the CHCl2 in product was derived solely from CHBrCl2?
3. The authors repeatedly emphasized the derivation potentials of CHCl2 group. Derivation experiments should be conducted, for example, convert CHCl2 to CHO, etc.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Relevant and interesting paper by Tsvelikhovsky and team.
The dichloromethylation of 6-membered ring enaminones is designed, analyzed and well described. Several parameters are considered, a robust mechanistic explanation is given and a number of functionalized derivatives (trans stereochemistry) are produced in a reliable manner. The text is well written, the figures are didactic, and the Supplementary Information is very illustrative, full of details, the new compounds well characterized and with high degree of purity (copies of the NMR spectra).
I find that the manuscript is a nice piece of work, and can be publishable, but in a specialized journal, devoted to Organic Chemistry (J. Org. Chem.; Org. Lett, Org. Biol. Chem., Adv. Synth. & Catal., etc.), but it lacks (in my opinion) novelty, generality and relevant synthetic applications to be published in Nat. Commun. Nevertheless, it is an important reaction, with suggestive implications, reflecting a serious research.
Points that may be addressed to raise scientific level and questions related.
a) Around 50 rxns of this type (HA addition to the double bond of 6-membered enaminones are described (a few organometallic couplings, and some radical additions, mostly). The processes described are new. However, the yield is, at most, 50%; in some cases, even lower.
Authors may check (computationally or by other means) why the “wrong” stereoisomer does not equilibrate with the productive one, being the addition step dynamic? Also, is this process suitable for a catalytic method?, as 2 equiv of proline are needed.
b) Only dichloromethylation? Why not other C+ species or even X+ or other electrophiles? The mechanism should be also operative, right? In this endeavor, the audience should have evidences (in this system) of the usefulness of a number of the described adducts. Please, show some examples of synthetically relevant transformations of the CHCl2 group (drugs, commodities, NPs, probes…) that justify the importance of the method.
b) Stereochemistry. Did authors rule out any stereochemical induction by proline in the generation of the new stereogenic centers (given a favored trans stereochemistry, if the C*-CHCl2 centre is controlled, may led to good overall stereoselection). This must be clearly stated (I do not find the sentence in the text). Incidentally, this would increase the value of the discoveries.
c) Scope. At the moment. quite restricted. Only 6-membered enaminones are analyzed (and other types of enaminones?). Also, the amine component lacks generality (NH, tert-groups, limitations in functionalizing complex residues linked to the N atom?). Incidentally, why compound 45 do not keep reacting to dichloromethylate the other enaminone group? The isolated yield is only 6%, And the rest?
I believe that if a relevant number of these issues would be successfully addressed, the manuscript may gbe publishable in Nat. Commun. Otherwise, in my opinion, it should be directed to a specialized journal.

Summary of key revisions and experimental additions
We thank all three reviewers for their thoughtful, constructive, and rigorous evaluations.
We begin by clarifying a central conceptual feature that may not have been sufficiently emphasized in the previous version:
this study introduces a new organocatalytic approach in which productive bond formation is governed not by conventional
catalyst-controlled asymmetry but by intermediate-level stereochemical resolution. This resolution-gated architecture enables
precise control, absolute site selectivity, high anti-diastereoselectivity (>99:1 dr), and closed-shell activation of halomethanes
under metal-free, radical-free, and light-free conditions, thereby defining the core innovation of the work.
Among the points raised, yield was noted as a limitation. We have optimized the transformation as far as possible, but it is
important to highlight that the ~50% yield reflects not a shortcoming of the method, but a direct and inherent consequence of
its resolution-based design. This yield reflects the selectivity-driven nature of the transformation, which operates by
fundamentally different principles from those of traditional catalytic cycles. While the transformation has an intrinsic yield
ceiling, it is operationally simple, proceeds cleanly, and affords stable products without competing side reactions.
Importantly, the reviewers’ feedback prompted us to explore the broader potential of this design, leading to the discovery of
an extended electrophilic polyhalomethylation manifold that substantially increases the scope and impact of the chemistry.
Our additions and strategic revisions include:
• Expanded scope & generality: A significant expansion of the main substrate scope (Figure 6), now incorporating
additional α-enaminones with varied N-substitution and ring systems. This includes an unprecedented demonstration of
electrophilic generality, wherein alternative dihalomethylating agents (CHBr₃, CBrCl₃, CHClBr₂) cleanly generate gem-
dibromo and mixed gem-halogenated products under unified, mild, and metal-free conditions.
• Novel divergent reactivity: The discovery of a previously unreported aromatization cascade unique to five-membered
α-enaminones, in which β-dichloromethylation triggers an in situ rearrangement culminating in novel substituted benzene
derivatives bearing both pyrrolidine and benzylamine functionalities (Figure 7).
• Enhanced synthetic utility: Detailed exploration of downstream derivatizations of b-dichloromethylated products
(Figure 7), demonstrating their synthetic versatility through oxidation, substitution, and elimination transformations.
• Mechanistic validation: Comprehensive mechanistic isotope-tracing experiments confirming that CHCl incorporation

significantly higher isolated yields for several representative products (see Supplementary Information).

To directly address the reviewer’s question regarding the origin of the CHCl₂ fragment, we performed a targeted isotopic

was analyzed by ¹H NMR, ²H NMR, and HRMS. The data revealed only trace incorporation of CDCl₂, despite the significant

and selectivity of the transformation.

most effective for probing primary isotope effects in rate-determining bond-breaking steps. Our transformation involves the

Comment 7: On page 6 of the manuscript, it is stated that complete conversion of starting material is observed, yielding a
clean 1:1 ratio of the desired product 17 and the corresponding secondary amine. I was wondering if you observe the other

Response: Mechanistically, the unproductive diastereomer undergoes fragmentation into a secondary amine and the parent
1,2-diketone. Although minor resonances of the diketone are observable by NMR in the crude mixture, its low abundance is
consistent with rapid secondary capture by the second equivalent of proline, which serves a dual functional role: promoting
the productive transformation and trapping the reactive dione fragment to prevent competitive side reactivity.
Under standard conditions, this buffer-like excess of proline engages the diketone to form highly polar, downstream species
such as enamines, iminium salts, or possibly oxazolidinone-type adducts. These species are not readily retained in the CHCl₃
phase and are therefore removed during aqueous workup. Their presence is occasionally detectable by 1H NMR in the crude
mixture as minor baseline features, but does not interfere with the isolation or quantification of the major products.
As shown in Figure 4C, the crude mixture shows a clean 1:1 ratio of product 17 to the liberated secondary amine 18. Residual
polar proline-dione adducts are observable as diffuse baselines, but no competing side products are evident. This further
supports the role of proline in fragment resolution and reinforces the process's clean selectivity.
The only other minor byproduct observed during the transformation is pyrroline 8 (Figure 4A), formed via decomposition of
proline itself. This species was independently verified and discussed in our response to Comment 4.

of known :CCl₂-derived byproducts (e.g., gem-dichlorocyclopropanes or tetrachloroethene), as confirmed by both ¹H NMR and
GC-MS analyses of crude mixtures.
Given the complete lack of productive reactivity under these conditions, we did not pursue further mechanistic investigation
into the involvement of carbene in these specific systems. The absence of both target and carbene-type side products strongly
suggests that even if :CCl₂ is generated, it does not engage productively with α-enaminones, which remain completely inert.
Instead, we emphasize that the observed reactivity arises uniquely under buffered conditions created by the cooperative
acid–base pairing of L-proline and K₃PO₄. This dual system, which we previously characterized (Chem. Sci. 2019, 10, 10267;
Green Chem. 2023, 25, 5916), appears essential for both activating the substrate and controlling the progression through the
stereochemically gated resolution pathway.

proline–enaminone intermediates (e.g., hydroxylamines 4a/4b) universally resulted in no reaction. These observations are

carbene chemistry.

were detected in crude mixtures or isolated fractions (NMR, GC-MS, HRMS analyses), further excluding a dichlorocarbene
mechanism.

• Mechanistic context. The observed “decomposition” corresponds to the programmed fragmentation of the mismatched
intermediate in a resolution-type pathway; only the matched partner advances to product. This stereochemical gate
intrinsically imposes a maximum yield of 50%.
• Targeted optimization to bias the equilibrium. Guided by the idea that acid release (HX) during the initial
condensation/proton-transfer events could influence the matched↔mismatched ratio, we introduced acid scavengers,
proton sponges, and anion-exchange/phase-transfer resins: DMAP, Amberlyst A26, AmberChrom 1×8, Amberlite IRA 400,
and 1,8-bis(dimethylamino)naphthalene to tilt the equilibrium toward the reactive pathway. These interventions produced
only modest effects; details and side-by-side comparisons are added to the SI.
• On practicality. While the yield is intrinsically governed by the resolution mechanism, this unique stereochemical gating
is precisely what enables the high selectivity without complex catalysts.
To balance this, we emphasize the operational simplicity:
- Metal/catalyst/ligand-free
- No strong acids/bases
- No inert atmosphere or photolysis
- Standard laboratory solvents and reagents: CHCl₃/proline/K₃PO₄
- Product isolation typically involves only solvent removal and filtration, affording clean, bench-stable β-CHCl₂ adducts
without chromatographic complexity.
- The liberated secondary amine is obtained in equimolar amounts and can be recovered.
- We also demonstrate concise derivatizations (e.g., vinyl chloride, acetal, ketal, enol ether), underscoring synthetic
utility. Importantly, the work establishes a previously unreported closed-shell electrophilic transfer of polyhalomethyl
units from haloform reagents.
Changes Made: We (i) state the resolution-imposed yield limit explicitly, (ii) summarize the equilibrium-bias additive screen
(full data in SI), and (iii) clarify operational simplicity, product stability, and downstream elaborations in the Results.
Comment 2: Why the reaction plateaued at 50% yield when using an equimolar mixture of L- and D-proline? While product 2
was obtained in 30% yield in the presence of only L-prolin?
Response: Proline (regardless of chirality) plays an indispensable, stoichiometric, and dual-functional role that lies outside
the classical catalytic framework. First, it facilitates the formation of stereochemically defined intermediates via reaction with
the α-enaminone. Second, and critically, it serves to trap the released 1,2-diketone fragment formed through fragmentation of
the non-productive diastereomer. This fragment-trapping step is not peripheral; it is mechanistically essential for stabilizing the
reaction outcome and ensuring a clean mass balance.
As such, a total of 2.0 equivalents of proline are required:
• 1.0 equiv. participates in the formation of the matched and mismatched intermediates.
• The remaining 1.0 equiv. is necessary to condense with and stabilize the liberated diketone fragments, preventing
decomposition or side reactions.
In the experiment using a 1:1 racemic mixture of L- and D-proline, only 1.0 equiv. is available for the initial condensation step.
Of this:
• 0.5 equiv. is L-proline → forms 0.25 equiv. of productive intermediate and 0.25 equiv. of non-productive.
• 0.5 equiv. is D-proline → forms 0.25 equiv. of productive and 0.25 equiv. of non-productive.
Thus, 0.5 equiv. of proline-derived intermediates are productive, and 0.5 equiv. are non-productive. Upon fragmentation, the
non-productive intermediates release 1,2-diketone, and the other 1.0 equiv. of racemic proline (which remains unreacted)
condenses with this diketone to stabilize it. Therefore, even in the racemic case, full material balance is preserved, and the
overall maximum yield plateaus at 50%, exactly matching the theoretical expectation of resolution.
This outcome is mechanistically identical to using 2.0 equiv. of enantiopure proline: one equivalent participates in intermediate
formation, while the second captures the byproduct.
Here, 1.5 equivalents of proline are the theoretical minimum:
• 1.0 equiv. for forming intermediates (matched + mismatched),
• 0.5 equiv. to trap the released diketone fragments from the non-productive intermediates.
However, we use an overall 2.0 equiv. In practice, to ensure complete conversion and buffer integrity, it is necessary to provide
operational robustness, excess trapping capacity, and avoid incomplete quenching of reactive byproducts.
This experiment was one of several conducted to support the bifurcation–resolution mechanism and directly illustrates the
structural gating that defines the yield ceiling.
Comment 3: CHCl3 can also be used as the CHCl2 source as listed in Figure 3. So, how can the authors deem the CHCl2 in
product was derived solely from CHBrCl2?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this meaningful and insightful comment. We agree that the original main text did not
sufficiently distinguish between the initial chloroform discovery experiment and the optimized CHBrCl₂ protocol, and we have
now clarified this in the revised manuscript.
We initially discovered the transformation serendipitously while using CHCl₃ as a solvent. However, despite its abundance,
CHCl₃ alone resulted in low yields and incomplete conversion. Upon switching to CHBrCl₂, we observed clean and complete
formation of the β-dichloromethylated product across a wide range of α-enaminone substrates.
To directly address the reviewer’s question regarding the origin of the CHCl₂ fragment, we performed a targeted isotopic
tracking experiment: CHBrCl₂ was used as the dichloromethyl donor in CDCl₃ as solvent, and the resulting product mixture
was analyzed by ¹H NMR, ²H NMR, and HRMS. The data revealed only trace incorporation of CDCl₂, despite the significant
excess of CDCl₃. This outcome confirms that CHBrCl₂, not CHCl₃, is the kinetically and mechanistically relevant CHCl₂ source.
Also, as part of our broader exploration, we examined whether alternative haloform-type donors (CHBr₃, CHClBr₂, CBrCl₃)
could deliver related transformations under otherwise identical proline-buffered conditions. In all cases, the expected geminal
di- or tri-halogenated products were obtained cleanly, without any CHCl₂ incorporation, further confirming the origin-specificity
and selectivity of the transformation.
We again thank the reviewer for highlighting this critical mechanistic point, which is now fully clarified in the revised manuscript.

General Comments: We thank the reviewer for constructive assessments. In light of the concerns raised, we have undertaken
substantial revisions to strengthen both the conceptual and experimental foundations of the work. The updated manuscript
and SI section now include expanded mechanistic analysis, clarification of key selectivity principles, additional control
experiments, and refinements to the presentation of scope and limitations, all of which align with the reviewer’s specific points.
These revisions substantially enhance the clarity, rigor, and contextual framing of the study. We believe the manuscript now
more clearly articulates the uniqueness and broader significance of this closed-shell electrophilic β-dihalomethylation manifold,
and we respectfully hope that the improvements satisfactorily address the issues raised and enable reconsideration for
publication in Nature Communications.
Comment 1: I find that the manuscript is a nice piece of work, and can be publishable, but in a specialized journal, devoted
to Organic Chemistry (J. Org. Chem.; Org. Lett, Org. Biol. Chem., Adv. Synth. & Catal., etc.), but it lacks (in my opinion)
novelty, generality and relevant synthetic applications to be published in Nat. Commun.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s upbeat assessment of the work’s quality. However, we respectfully
maintain that the conceptual and mechanistic innovations reported here are appropriate for the broad readership of Nature
Communications. We believe the initial manuscript may not have sufficiently highlighted the fundamental departure this method
takes from established reactivity modes. We have revised the Introduction and Discussion to frame these advances, which
are summarized below explicitly:
1. First closed-shell electrophilic polyhalomethylation: To date, the transfer of di- or trihalomethyl units (e.g., CHCl₂,
CBrCl) has been exclusively the domain of radical or carbene chemistry. This work reports the first example of a two-
electron, closed-shell transfer of these fragments from stable haloforms, including the demonstration that CHBr₃,
CBrCl₃, and CHClBr₂ can also be effectively employed to generate gem-dibromo, mixed gem-halides, and other polyhalogenated
products under these unified conditions. This establishes a fundamentally new mechanistic manifold — an "electrophilic
haloform" pathway - without precedent in the literature.
2. Umpolung of a historically inert scaffold: alpha-Enaminones are classically resistant to electrophilic functionalization
due to their electronic bias. By leveraging a transient umpolung strategy, we unlock a general entry point for beta-
functionalization that has previously been inaccessible, solving a long-standing reactivity challenge for this substrate class.
3. Diastereomeric gating mechanism: The selectivity in this transformation arises from a rare "stereochemical resolution"
mechanism mediated by proline, rather than traditional transition-state control. This conceptual finding, where an
organocatalyst acts as a diastereomer-selective gatekeeper for reactive intermediates, adds a new dimension to how
selectivity can be engineered in cascade sequences.
4. Discovery of a size-dependent aromatization cascade: Prompted by the reviewer’s comments on scope, we have
uncovered that 5-membered rings undergo a unique, spontaneous aromatization cascade following dichloromethylation
(now detailed in Figure 7). This divergence in reactivity adds significant depth to the study, offering a rapid, metal-free route
to fused heteroaromatics.
We believe that establishing a new electrophilic manifold for haloforms, solving a reactivity problem in conjugated systems,
and defining a new mode of stereocontrol constitutes a foundational advance rather than an incremental one.
Changes Made: The Introduction and Discussion sections of the manuscript have been thoroughly revised to explicitly frame
these key conceptual advances, aligning with points 1-4. (See Main Text, Introduction, and Discussion sections).
Comment 2: Around 50 rxns of this type (HA addition to the double bond of 6-membered enaminones are described (a few
organometallic couplings, and some radical additions, mostly). The processes described are new. However, the yield is,
at most, 50%; in some cases, even lower.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this point regarding precedent. We have conducted an exhaustive search of the
literature and were unable to locate the specific examples of HA-type additions to cyclic alpha-enaminones under closed-shell
conditions referenced in the comment. While radical or organometallic functionalizations of simple enones exist, the direct,
metal-free electrophilic functionalization of the ambident alpha-enaminone system remains, to our knowledge, unreported.
Regarding the yield, the reviewer is correct that the isolated yields generally plateau at approximately 50%. As we now clarify
in the revised text, this is not a failure of conversion but an intrinsic feature of the mechanistic resolution. The reaction is
designed to filter a racemic mixture through a diastereoselective gate, where only the "matched" intermediate progresses to
product. While this imposes a theoretical yield ceiling, the trade-off provides high diastereoselectivity and clean reactivity
profiles without the need for expensive chiral ligands, transition metals, or complex purification. We argue that this operational
simplicity and mechanistic uniqueness offer significant value despite the resolution-limited yield.

mechanistic probing, additional synthesis, and the development of new downstream transformations. The additional studies
strengthened the manuscript substantially, expanding the mechanistic foundation, revealing new reactivity regimes, and

characterization, and revised Figures 6 and 7. We hope that the depth and completeness of the revisions clarify the conceptual
significance of the discovery and place the manuscript on firm footing for publication in Nature Communications.
